query: For high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles intended for catalysis, sensing, energy storage, corrosion-related uses, and other applications requiring thermal stability, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their premelting and melting behavior and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing factor, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Premelting and melting in high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles are governed primarily by surface energy heterogeneity induced by local lattice distortions and selective elemental segregation. High configurational entropy creates non-uniform bonding environments that promote enrichment of lower-cohesive-energy elements at the nanoparticle surface, which in turn lowers the energy barrier for surface premelting relative to lower-entropy or bulk materials.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniformly synthesized HEA nanoparticles (5–8 nearly equimolar elements) immobilized on inert supports, with typical sizes in the 10–50 nm range.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the degree of configurational entropy by comparing full HEA nanoparticle compositions with analogues containing fewer elements (e.g., binary or ternary alloys) prepared under otherwise identical conditions.
generation.conditions: Experiments performed under controlled inert atmospheres with a well-calibrated temperature ramp (using DSC and in situ TEM) over the premelting to melting temperature range (approximately 200–500 °C for these nanoparticles); complementary surface analyses (e.g., EDS, XPS) are conducted while ensuring similar particle size distributions for fair comparison.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions (strain fields) and selective elemental segregation at the nanoparticle surface which create heterogeneous surface energies.
generation.mechanism: The high mixing entropy in HEA nanoparticles induces a ‘frozen’ chemical disorder that results in local differences in atomic size and bonding. This promotes preferential migration or segregation of elements with lower cohesive or melting enthalpies to the surface. These segregated regions then exhibit reduced cohesive energy, triggering an earlier onset of surface premelting. By contrast, lower-entropy nanoparticles with fewer elements form more uniform surfaces with higher effective melting points.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical heating conditions, full HEA nanoparticles will exhibit a lower onset temperature for surface premelting (and consequently a lower overall melting temperature), supported by direct imaging of a premelted surface layer and by compositional analysis showing surface enrichment of specific lower-melting-point elements. Reduced-entropy nanoparticles (binary/ternary alloys) should show a delayed premelting onset and more uniform composition.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles made of fewer constituent elements (e.g., binary or ternary alloys) under the same synthesis and processing conditions, which are expected to have more uniform surface composition and higher premelting/melting temperatures.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to hold for nanoparticles in the size range of roughly 5–100 nm and for compositions where high configurational entropy drives significant local lattice distortions. For substantially larger (bulk) materials or ultra-small clusters (<5 nm), additional size-dependent or quantum effects may come into play, and the hypothesis may not apply.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative role of each individual element’s segregation behavior and the precise magnitude of the induced lattice strain remain uncertain. It is also unclear how support interactions may modify the observed premelting behavior, and these factors need to be isolated in further studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles: one set with full HEA composition (5–8 elements) and a second set with reduced composition (binary or ternary alloys), all immobilized on the same type of inert support and with similar particle size distributions. Subject both sets to controlled temperature ramping experiments using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and in situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to monitor the onset and progression of surface premelting. Concurrently, perform surface composition analysis (e.g., EDS, XPS) at various temperatures to detect any elemental segregation at the nanoparticle surfaces.
measurements: DSC thermograms to precisely determine the premelting and melting onset temperatures
In situ TEM imaging to identify and measure the extent of surface premelting layers
EDS or XPS mapping to assess changes in surface elemental composition
Particle size distribution measurements to confirm comparability between samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If full HEA nanoparticles do not consistently display a statistically significant lower premelting/melting onset temperature and lack measurable selective elemental segregation on their surfaces compared to the reduced-entropy nanoparticles, then the hypothesis that surface energy heterogeneity driven by configurational entropy governs premelting behavior would be falsified.

High-entropy alloys, containing five or even more metals, have attracted significant attentions, because of their unique chemical and physical complexity, which endow alloys with tunable features and properties such as thermal stability, superior corrosion resistance, high hardness, exceptional ductility, and superparamagnetism. A wide range of researches have revealed that the nanoparticles loading on the supports could significantly improve specific surface area and surface energy compared with the bulk materials or the nanoparticles themselves,. In addition, in industrial applications, the nanoparticles need to be dispersedly immobilized on granular supports, such as Al2O3, zeolite, and carbon materials etc., which can make the catalysts feature with tunable size, shape, and stability, enhancing the catalytic performance. Therefore, the supported high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA-NPs) can be promisingly applied in catalysis, chemical sensing, biology, and energy conversion. However, the common extreme high temperature related approaches such as arc melting and laser cladding are not suitable for supporting HEA-NPs due to the rapid growth and aggregation of nanoparticles.
